newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak parliament to debate controversial law.
newsitem.headline: Slovak parliament to debate controversial law.

text.p: The Slovak parliament this week will re-open debate on an amendment to the criminal code allowing the punishment of organisers of anti-government rallies or those spreading false information abroad.

Parliamentary Chairman Ivan Gasparovic said on Monday the controversial law, known as the anti-subversion law or the law on protection of the republic, was included on the agenda at the request of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar's governing coalition.
"I have included this law on the agenda of the October session at the explicit request of the (ruling) coalition," Gasparovic told a news conference.
The amendment was originally approved in March, but later returned to parliament by President Michal Kovac for revision.
The government is expected to use its majority to push the law through parliament, which opens the session on Tuesday, over-riding Kovac.

The amendment, drafted on the initiative of junior coalition member, the far-right Slovak National Party (SNS), defines as a crime "organised public rallies aimed at subverting the constitutional system...the defence ability of the country or at destroying its independence".
According to the amended law, offenders face jail terms of up to three years or fines. If the crime is committed by "an organised group" punishment can rise to as high as five years.

The legislation has sparked protests from opposition members and the Roman Catholic Church, who claim parts of it resembled catch-all anti-subversion laws used to crush dissent before the fall of communism in 1989.
But Meciar and his allies, facing increasing international criticism for the country's human rights record, have said the law cannot be used against the political opponents.

"There is no danger of political trials...it is nonsense," Gasparovic said. "But Slovakia is a young state and must have some tools to defend itself against those who want to take actions against its statehood," he added.
However Gasparovic, a lawyer who did not support the amendment in the first vote, hinted the law could be used to stifle some aspirations of the country's 600,000 strong ethnic Hungarian minority.
"I abstained in March, but if I had known what would happen later during the Budapest conference...I would have probably pushed the "yes' button," he said.

A conference organised by the Hungarian government in July called the "Hungarian Summit", issued a communique calling for autonomy of ethnic Hungarian minorities as a "basic condition for retaining the identity of Hungarians living abroad."
Slovakia reacted with anger, saying Hungarian officials attending the conference had signed the communique, thereby violating a basic relations treaty between the two countries.
